summary: cargo test failure is silently masked by `|| true`, so the extraction oracle always exits 0 (green) even when Rust diverges from the extracted Coq proof.
evidence: Lines 40-41 of the committed script (HEAD d234f30a49): `( cd "$ROOT" && RUSTC_WRAPPER= cargo test -p unlace-ir --test extraction_oracle -- --nocapture 2>&1 | grep -E "extraction_oracle:|test result:" || true )`. With `set -euo pipefail` (line 15), when `cargo test` exits 1 and `grep` finds "test result: FAILED" and exits 0, `pipefail` selects the pipeline exit as 1. The compound `pipeline || true` converts that to 0. The subshell exits 0, the script prints "extraction_oracle: done." unconditionally, exits 0, and `quality_axes.sh` (which invokes it at line 43 under its own `set -euo pipefail`) reports the axis as passing. category: test coverage gap / false conformance guarantee
summary: The extraction oracle only ever constructs fully-known KnownBits inputs via fc_zero/fc_one, so the both_known gate in kxor is always the full mask — the partial-knowledge transfer path (zero|one < mask) is never exercised. The oracle advertised as the "deepest conformance layer" only validates constant-folding agreement, not the general transfer function behavior the proofs are actually about.
evidence: oracle_driver.ml lines 47–50 derive all inputs via `fc_zero`/`fc_one`: `az = O.fc_zero (big_of_unsigned xa) bw`, `ao = O.fc_one xa bw`, `bz = O.fc_zero xb bw`, `bo = O.fc_one xb bw`. By the algebraic identity fc_zero(v,w) | fc_one(v,w) = (~v & mask) | (v & mask) = mask, both az|ao and bz|bo are always the full width mask. kxor_bothknown (Extract.v L29–30, knownbits_oracle.ml L662–663) is therefore always mask, making the `& both_known` gating in kxor_one/kxor_zero a no-op AND for every generated vector. The partial-knowledge regime — where bz|bo < mask zeros out genuinely unknown XOR output bits — is never reached. Python verification confirms: for a partial input (bz=0b11000000, bo=0b00000011, w=8), both_known=0b11000011 ≠ 0xFF and xor output differs materially, but oracle_driver.ml cannot produce such inputs. extraction_oracle.rs (lines 58–59) also exclusively calls `KnownBits::from_constant`, so the Rust test inherits the same blind spot. docs/formal-verification.md L50–62 calls this oracle the "deepest conformance layer" that catches "any divergence between the production Rust and the proved definition", but this claim is only true for the constant-folding (fully-known) subset of the transfer function's input domain.

summary: random_struct never generates overlapping fields, so best_fit_tightest is never exercised and the tightness tie-break is dead code under the generator
evidence: In random_struct() (lines 43–55), cursor starts at 0. Each iteration first does `cursor += rng.next() % 4` (adds 0–3 bytes, always ≥ 0), sets `offset = cursor`, pushes a field there, then sets `cursor = offset + width as u64`. Because the gap added before the next field is non-negative, the next field's start is always ≥ the previous field's end. Fields are therefore strictly non-overlapping: at most one field ever covers any given byte offset. Consequently: (1) coq_expected_offset()'s `.max()` on line 91 always selects from a singleton-or-empty set and never resolves a tie; (2) get_best_fit_member()'s tie-break branch (`Some(prev) if f.offset > prev.offset => best = Some(f)`, tinfo.rs line 244) can never fire; (3) the best_fit_tightest property — which is only non-trivial when 2+ fields cover the same offset — is never put under any pressure. The comment on line 37 reads "possibly-overlapping fields" but the construction makes overlap impossible by construction. The test passes vacuously with respect to the tightness property it claims to pin.

summary: check_transitivity is tautological: it derives both sides from the same idom chain, so it cannot detect a build_dominator_tree that returns a structurally valid but semantically wrong dominator tree
evidence: dominates(dom, d, n) (line 70) walks the idom chain from n to root; d dominates n iff d appears on that chain. check_transitivity(dom, blocks, b, id) (line 99) asserts: for all d where dominates(dom,d,id), also dominates(dom,d,b), where id=dom.idom(b) is the parent of b in the idom tree. Walking the chain from b gives b→id→idom(id)→…→root, so any ancestor d of id is necessarily also an ancestor of b — this is a pure tree-structural identity that holds for ANY idom mapping regardless of correctness w.r.t. the actual CFG. The test never constructs an independent CFG-path-based oracle (no traversal of bb.successors/predecessors), so it cannot catch build_dominator_tree (line 1689, which calls petgraph's simple_fast) producing a well-formed idom tree encoding the wrong dominance relation. The only non-tautological check is check_antisym (cycle detection, line 106).

summary: reachable_blocks() uses the dominator tree under test as its own reachability oracle, so a mis-pruning bug in build_dominator_tree is invisible to check_tree_laws
evidence: reachable_blocks (line 89–95) defines the checked set as blocks where `b == dom.root() || dom.idom(b).is_some()` — entirely derived from the DominatorTree being verified. check_tree_laws (line 115) then only asserts poset laws over that set. No independent BFS/DFS on the raw CFG graph is performed. Concrete consequence: if build_dominator_tree (ssa.rs:1694–1702) omits a CFG-reachable block from the idom BTreeMap — e.g., due to a petgraph simple_fast edge-case or a node_map lookup miss — reachable_blocks silently excludes it from `blocks`, all assertions in the loop at line 116 skip that block, and the test passes without detecting the mismatch. The CFG does contain all n blocks as nodes (build_cfg inserts every func.blocks entry), so there is a well-defined ground-truth reachability set derivable from the graph that the test never consults.

summary: random_struct never generates overlapping fields, so the best_fit_tightest tie-breaking logic in tinfo.rs is never exercised and is mutation-invisible to the conformance test.
evidence: At line 55, `cursor = offset + width as u64` sets cursor to the end of the current field. Line 46 then adds `rng.next() % 4` (range 0–3) on top, so every subsequent field starts at `prev_end + gap` where `gap >= 0`. This makes it arithmetically impossible for any two fields to overlap. The docstring at line 37 states "possibly-overlapping fields" but the invariant is never satisfied. Consequently, for every random struct, at most one field's range contains any queried offset, making `coq_expected_offset(fields, off).max()` a trivial single-element max. The tie-breaking branch in tinfo.rs lines 242–246 (`Some(prev) if f.offset > prev.offset => best = Some(f)`) is never evaluated. Deleting that entire arm and returning the *first* containing field instead would leave all 200,000 iterations of `tinfo_best_fit_matches_coq_spec` passing unchanged — a high-severity survivable mutation that directly undermines the `best_fit_tightest` property the test claims to pin.

summary: Conformance test never checks idom minimality (closest strict dominator), so an over-conservative idom (e.g. always entry) passes every assertion despite being a wrong dominator tree.
evidence: check_tree_laws asserts only: dom_refl (dominates(b,b)), entry_dominates (dominates(root,b)), `dominates(idom(b), b)` (line 122), one-step transitivity along the idom chain (check_transitivity), and antisymmetry (check_antisym). None constrain idom to be the CLOSEST strict dominator. The Coq spec it claims conformance with — rocq-tests/theories/DominatorTree.v, `Definition idom (d n) := strictly_dominates d n /\ forall d', strictly_dominates d' n -> dominates d' d` — requires that minimality/closure clause. Verified counterexample on linear CFG 0->1->2->3: corrupting idoms to idom(1)=idom(2)=idom(3)=0 (every block immediately dominated by entry) yields chains [1,0],[2,0],[3,0]; then dominates(idom(b),b) is true for all b (entry is on every chain), entry_dominates holds, refl holds, transitivity for id=root only ranges over d=root (true), and antisym holds since only entry dominates others. All assertions PASS while the tree is wrong (idom(2) should be 1, idom(3) should be 2).

summary: formal-verification.md line 70 claims RecordLayout's aligned/disjoint invariants are "exercised via DataLayout above" and labels the binding "spec + DataLayout binding", but layout_conformance.rs tests only data_layout.rs::{type_size,type_align} over arbitrary offsets and never touches abi_layout.rs::compute_record_layout (the actual shipping implementation of layout_fields). None of RecordLayout.v's three theorems are conformance-bound, so the binding is effectively spec-only and the doc overstates it.
evidence: RecordLayout.v (rocq-tests/theories/RecordLayout.v) proves layout_fields_aligned (line 123), layout_fields_disjoint (line 136), and align_to_least / greedy minimality (line 72). Its header (lines 3-5) explicitly states it mirrors crates/unlace-passes/src/abi_layout.rs, NOT data_layout.rs. abi_layout.rs::compute_record_layout (line 71) is the real shipping greedy-aligned placement routine (lines 86-96: aligns current_offset to each field's alignment, places, advances cursor) — a separate function that exists, contradicting line 70's "no separate shipping fn". layout_conformance.rs imports only data_layout::DataLayout (line 15) and exercises type_size/type_align (e.g. lines 90-101, 152-167); random_fields (lines 47-59) generates ascending, arbitrarily-gapped, NON-aligned offsets (off += 1 + rng.next() % 16), so the tested structs are not RecordLayout-placed layouts. `grep -rl abi_layout crates/unlace-ir/tests/` returns nothing — no conformance test references abi_layout.rs. Thus the three RecordLayout theorems (aligned placed offsets, disjointness, greedy minimality) are unexercised by any Rust test, and the DataLayout tests cannot cover them because they never invoke the placement function.

summary: Guard overflow silently returns false instead of panicking, converting any idom-chain anomaly into a misleading entry_dominates failure
evidence: Lines 80–86 confirmed verbatim: `guard += 1; if guard > 10_000 { break; }` followed by `return false`. If the idom chain walk ever fails to reach `d` or `dom.root()` within 10,000 steps (e.g., due to an idom cycle or a bug where a non-root block has no idom path to root), `dominates` returns `false`. The call site at line 119 — `assert!(dominates(dom, dom.root(), b), "entry_dominates: {b:?}")` — then fires with a message blaming entry-dominates rather than exposing the underlying anomaly. CFGs generated here are 3–10 blocks, so a correct idom chain is at most 9 hops; the 10,000 guard is ~1,000× too large and masks bugs for thousands of wasted iterations before producing a wrong diagnosis.

summary: datalayout_array_size_and_align is a tautological self-check: both assertions compare the implementation to itself rather than to an independent specification.
evidence: In data_layout.rs line 62, DataLayout::type_size for Type::Array{element, size: Some(count)} is literally `self.type_size(element)?.checked_mul(*count)`. The test (layout_conformance.rs lines 117–122) captures `es = dl.type_size(&elem)` then asserts `dl.type_size(&arr) == es.checked_mul(len)` — these are identical computations. Similarly, type_align for Type::Array (data_layout.rs line 85) is `self.type_align(element)`, and the test asserts `dl.type_align(&arr) == dl.type_align(&elem)` (lines 124–128), which is again the same expression on both sides. A bug that changes the array-size formula (e.g. replacing multiplication with addition) would update both sides of the assertion equally and would not be caught.

summary: check_struct_size_bounds and check_struct_align are algebraic tautologies given the DataLayout implementation and cannot fail without a full rewrite of type_size/type_align for structs.
evidence: DataLayout::type_size for Struct (data_layout.rs line 64–67) folds over field.offset + type_size(field.ty) with max, so its result is max(offset_i + size_i) over all fields — every individual summand is ≤ the result by definition. check_struct_size_bounds (layout_conformance.rs line 136) asserts `f.offset + fsz <= ssize` which is just asserting a summand ≤ its own max-fold. DataLayout::type_align for Struct (data_layout.rs line 86–91) folds over type_align(field.ty) with max; check_struct_align (line 144–145) asserts `fa <= salign`, i.e. a term ≤ its own maximum. Both assertions are guaranteed to pass by the very arithmetic definition of max — they cannot distinguish a correct from a subtly broken implementation unless the folding strategy is changed entirely.

summary: The binding-strength ledger row for `RecordLayout` aligned/disjoint claims its invariants are "exercised via DataLayout above," but RecordLayout.v actually mirrors the greedy field-placement algorithm `abi_layout.rs::compute_record_layout` (offset cursor + alignment padding), whose aligned-placement, disjointness, and greedy-minimality proofs are not tested by layout_conformance.rs, which only queries DataLayout::type_size/type_align on caller-constructed types.
evidence: RecordLayout.v line 3-6: "Mirrors the greedy ABI field-layout computation in [crates/unlace-passes/src/abi_layout.rs]". It proves layout_fields_aligned (placed offsets aligned), layout_fields_disjoint (distinct placed fields non-overlapping), and align_to_least (greedy minimality) over a `layout_fields`/`align_to` construction. abi_layout.rs::compute_record_layout (lines 71-101) is the matching Rust placement algorithm: it tracks current_offset and pads with `current_offset += align - misalign`. By contrast layout_conformance.rs only calls DataLayout::type_size/type_align on Type values whose field offsets are caller-supplied (random_fields sets `offset` directly); it never invokes or checks any placement/disjointness algorithm. Thus the doc's "exercised via DataLayout above" binding points at the wrong Rust module, and compute_record_layout has no conformance test against RecordLayout.v.

summary: The comment on line 37 claims the generator produces 'possibly-overlapping fields', but the loop logic at lines 43–55 guarantees fields are always non-overlapping. cursor is set to offset + width after each field, so the next field always starts at or after the end of the previous one. The tightest-fit tiebreak (best_fit_tightest in TInfo.v) — which selects the highest-offset containing field among overlapping candidates — is therefore never exercised by this generator.
evidence: Line 37: '// Build a random flat struct: ascending, possibly-gapped, possibly-overlapping'. Loop body (lines 43–55): cursor starts at 0; line 46 adds 0–3 bytes gap; line 48 sets offset = cursor; line 55 sets cursor = offset + width. Since cursor always advances to the end of each field before the next is placed, two consecutive fields can be adjacent but never overlapping. The coq_expected_offset reference implementation (lines 86–92) uses .max() to pick the highest-offset containing field, but with non-overlapping fields there is at most one containing field per offset, making the tiebreak dead code under current test inputs.

summary: field_ranges() uses unwrap_or(1) for None-size fields while calc_gaps() uses unwrap_or(0) and skips zero-size fields — oracle and implementation diverge for any field whose TInfo::size() returns None
evidence: Confirmed in repository: tinfo_conformance.rs line 70: `.map(|f| (f.offset, f.offset + f.ty.size().unwrap_or(1)))` treats a None-size field as 1-byte wide. Production calc_gaps (tinfo.rs lines 363–366): `let f_size = f.ty.size().unwrap_or(0); if f_size > 0 { covered.push((f.offset, f.offset + f_size)); }` — excludes None-size fields entirely from coverage. The gap disjoint test (lines 121–135) compares calc_gaps output against field_ranges; if any field has None size, field_ranges records [offset, offset+1) but calc_gaps emits a gap covering that byte, producing a spurious test failure rather than catching a real bug. Currently dormant: random_struct (lines 39–64) calls int_ty() exclusively, producing TInfo::Int fields whose size() always returns Some(n) ∈ {1,2,4,8}, so the unwrap_or fallback is never reached today.

summary: The overlap-merge path in calc_gaps (cursor = cursor.max(*end)) is structurally unreachable under random_struct's generator AND unmodeled by the Coq gap_uncovered theorem, leaving a mutation-invisible hole in both the conformance test and the formal proof.
evidence:
1. random_struct (lines 43–55): cursor starts at 0, advances by `rng.next() % 4` (≥ 0 gap), field is placed at cursor, then cursor is immediately set to `offset + width`. Every new field therefore starts at or after the end of the previous one — fields are strictly disjoint. The doccomment on line 37 says "possibly-overlapping" but the code structurally contradicts that claim; no overlap is ever generated across 200,000 iterations.

2. calc_gaps (tinfo.rs 370–382): `cursor = cursor.max(*end)` is the overlap-merge guard. It only produces a result different from `cursor = *end` when `*end < cursor` (i.e., the incoming range is wholly subsumed by what is already merged). Because random_struct guarantees `*start >= previous *end` and ranges are sorted, `*end` is always ≥ cursor at the point of update. The max() never short-circuits; replacing it with `cursor = *end` is semantically identical on all generated inputs. A mutation deleting the merge would pass every test.

3. Coq TInfo.v gap_uncovered (line 189) proves only: if `o < f_off f` for every field `f`, then `o` is not covered — that is, a byte strictly below all field starts is uncovered (the leading-gap case). trailing_gap_uncovered (line 199) covers the mirror case above all ends. The prose comment (lines 170–183) explicitly states the model does NOT prove the merge loop, covering only "the canonical two-field adjacency." No Coq theorem models what gap_uncovered yields for an offset lying between two ranges where a third overlapping range has already advanced the cursor.

4. The conformance test at line 119 (tinfo_calc_gaps_disjoint_from_fields) therefore never exercises the one code path — overlap-merge — that distinguishes calc_gaps from a trivially simpler implementation, and the Coq side provides no compensating proof for that path.

summary: Ledger row claims conformance binding for get_best_fit_member/calc_gaps wholesale, but the 400K-case conformance suite only exercises the flat-struct-of-ints path; Union/Array/Qualified branches of get_best_fit_member are unreached by the generator.
evidence: Line 67: `| TInfo.best_fit / calc_gaps | tinfo.rs::{get_best_fit_member,calc_gaps} | conformance (tinfo_conformance.rs, 400K cases) |`. summary: The `dominates` helper is defined by walking the idom chain itself, making all checked poset laws structural tautologies of any acyclic parent-pointer tree — the test cannot detect wrong-but-tree-shaped idom values
evidence: Lines 70–87: `dominates(dom, d, n)` walks `n`'s `idom` parents to root and returns true iff `d` appears on that chain. Every property then checked is a structural consequence of any rooted, acyclic parent-pointer tree: reflexivity (line 118) fires trivially on first comparison; entry-dominates-all (line 119) holds for any chain that eventually reaches `dom.root()`; transitivity (lines 99–103) reduces to "ancestors of a node include all ancestors of its parent"; antisymmetry (lines 106–112) merely excludes idom cycles, which cannot occur in a tree. A `build_ssa` that assigned each non-root block `idom = root` (a star topology, maximally wrong) would pass all 4K iterations without triggering a single assertion. The test file header (lines 1–9) and the inline comment at line 68 are both honest about this, but `formal-verification.md` line 68 describes the binding as "`DominatorTree` poset/idom … via `build_ssa`" and `COVERAGE.md` line 107 says "DominatorTree poset laws via real `build_ssa`, 4K CFGs" — framing that overstates the binding since no path-reachability ground truth is compared.

summary: check_tree_laws never verifies the immediacy (closest-dominator) property of idom(), so a wrong-but-self-consistent idom tree cannot be falsified by any assertion in the test.
evidence: The `dominates()` helper (lines 70–87) is derived entirely from the Rust idom-chain: it walks `n`'s idom-parents and returns true if `d` appears. Every assertion in `check_tree_laws` (lines 114–127) — dom_refl, entry_dominates, "idom dominates node" (line 122), check_transitivity, check_antisym — is evaluated within this self-referential system. A tree where `idom(b) == root` for every non-root block b would satisfy: `dominates(b, b)` (immediate match), `dominates(root, b)` (one step to root), `dominates(idom(b), b)` = `dominates(root, b)` (true), transitivity (trivially, only root dominates anything beyond self), and antisymmetry (no mutual domination in a flat tree). Nowhere does the test check that no block d' exists satisfying `strictly_dominates(d', b) && strictly_dominates(idom(b), d')`, which is exactly the Coq `idom` definition at DominatorTree.v line 156–158: `forall d', strictly_dominates d' n -> dominates d' d`. The test is thus blind to an idom tree that is internally consistent but wrong with respect to CFG path reachability.

summary: datalayout_struct_bounds_and_align is tautological: both check_struct_size_bounds and check_struct_align assert inequalities that are algebraically guaranteed by the definition of max in the very Rust implementation they query, so neither assertion can ever fail regardless of any bug.
evidence: data_layout.rs lines 64–67: `type_size` for `Type::Struct` returns `fields.iter().map(|f| f.offset.checked_add(type_size(f.ty)?)).try_fold(0, |m,e| e.map(|e| m.max(e)))` — i.e. `max_f(f.offset + type_size(f.ty))`. layout_conformance.rs lines 133–138 (`check_struct_size_bounds`) then asserts `f.offset + fsz <= ssize` where `fsz = dl.type_size(&f.ty)` and `ssize = dl.type_size(&s)` — reducing to asserting each summand is ≤ its own maximum, which is x ≤ max(x) — unfalsifiable. Identically, data_layout.rs lines 86–91: `type_align` for `Type::Struct` returns `max_f(type_align(f.ty))` (fold starting at 1). layout_conformance.rs lines 142–147 (`check_struct_align`) asserts `fa <= salign` where `fa = dl.type_align(&f.ty)` and `salign = dl.type_align(&s)` — again x ≤ max(x). Both `try_fold` calls propagate `None` so whenever the outer `Option` is `Some`, every constituent field call also returned `Some`, leaving no escape. A bug returning `struct_size * 2` or `struct_align * 2` would pass silently; only under-reporting bugs would fail.

summary: random_struct generates only strictly non-overlapping fields, despite the comment on line 37 claiming "possibly-overlapping". This excludes testing the overlap-handling logic that the Coq proofs explicitly cover.
evidence: The random_struct function (lines 43-64) initializes cursor=0 and advances it by field_width after each field (line 55: cursor = offset + width as u64). For field i+1, the offset is cursor plus a gap of 0-3 bytes (line 46: cursor += rng.next() % 4). This guarantees offset_{i+1} >= offset_i + width_i, ensuring strict non-overlap. In calc_gaps (tinfo.rs:377), the line cursor = cursor.max(*end) exists to handle overlapping ranges during the merge phase. For non-overlapping ranges where end_i <= start_{i+1}, this max() is always a no-op—the cursor already equals the previous end, and *end is the next field's end. Similarly, in get_best_fit_member (tinfo.rs:244), the tie-break condition f.offset > prev.offset only matters when multiple fields contain the same offset (overlap case). With non-overlapping fields, at most one field covers any given offset, so the tie-break is never triggered. The COVERAGE.md line 105 and formal-verification.md line 67 claim "400K cases"—this is 200K iterations each of best_fit and calc_gaps, all generated by the same non-overlapping pattern. The TInfo.v Coq proof (lines 45-46) explicitly states "selection proofs do NOT assume the field list is sorted", meaning the proofs prove correctness over arbitrary permutations and overlapping layouts, neither of which are exercised by the conformance tests.

summary: Binding ledger row `DominatorTree poset/idom` claims full conformance for `idom`, but the conformance test only verifies that `idom(b)` is *a* dominator of `b` — it never tests the immediacy (tightest-fit) condition that distinguishes `idom` from any other strict dominator.

summary: When both the two-successor branch (line 51) and the back-edge branch (line 56) fire for the same block, the back-edge is pushed to succs[2], but the Cbranch handler in cfg.rs reads only successors.first() (index 0) and successors.get(1) (index 1), silently dropping ~10% of intended back-edges and making loop-dominance coverage lower than the comment claims.

summary: COVERAGE.md's summary claim that "every public proven core is now tied to its live Rust counterpart by a machine-checked conformance test" overstates binding strength: the struct size/align checks in layout_conformance.rs are tautological against the Rust max-fold definitions, and dominator_conformance.rs does not test the idom-immediacy/uniqueness property attributed to it in row 10.

(2) DominatorTree.v proves `idom_unique` (line 164) where idom is the CLOSEST strict dominator (lines 154-156). summary: datalayout_array_size_and_align test assertions are tautological — both size and align checks re-derive from the same implementation path rather than an independent oracle
evidence: Confirmed by reading both files. Size assertion (lines 117–122): `data_layout.rs:62` implements `type_size(Array{elem, Some(count)})` as `self.type_size(element)?.checked_mul(*count)`. The test computes `es = dl.type_size(&elem)` and asserts `dl.type_size(&arr) == es.checked_mul(len)` — this is `(type_size(elem) * len) == (type_size(elem) * len)`, an identity. Align assertion (lines 124–128): `data_layout.rs:85` implements `type_align(Array{element,..})` as `self.type_align(element)` — a direct delegation. The test asserts `dl.type_align(&arr) == dl.type_align(&elem)`, which expands to `type_align(elem) == type_align(elem)`. A buggy implementation returning e.g. `elem_size * (len + 1)` or double the element alignment would pass both assertions unchanged, since no independent expected value is computed.

summary: datalayout_struct_bounds_and_align asserts properties that are definitionally true given the implementation, so the test has no power to detect layout bugs.
evidence: In data_layout.rs, struct size (lines 64-67) is `fields.iter().map(|f| f.offset + type_size(f.ty)).try_fold(0, max)` and struct align (lines 86-91) is `fields.iter().map(type_align).try_fold(1, max)`. The test's check_struct_size_bounds (lines 133-138) recomputes `type_size(f.ty)` and asserts `f.offset + fsz <= ssize`, where ssize is exactly that max-fold — so the asserted value is one of the elements the max was taken over, making `element <= max(set)` a tautology. check_struct_align (lines 141-147) asserts `fa <= salign` against the max of field aligns — also definitionally true. Both pass for any correct OR buggy max-folding implementation; they cannot catch off-by-one in field end, a wrong base case, or wrong reduction operator. The mirrored Coq theorem struct_size_bounds_member (DataLayout.v:121-123) is itself provable only because lsize for LStruct (DataLayout.v:30) is *defined* as that same max-fold, so the Rust test inherits the tautology.

summary: check_tree_laws inspects only the DominatorTree in isolation; all checks except entry_dominates are tautologically true for any acyclic rooted tree, regardless of whether idom assignments are correct w.r.t. the CFG
evidence: Verified against the actual file (line 99–127). `check_transitivity(dom, blocks, b, id)` where `id = dom.idom(b)`: collects every `d` where `dominates(d, id)` holds, then asserts `dominates(d, b)`. Since `dominates` walks the idom chain from a node to root, the idom-chain of `b` is `b → id → … → root` and the idom-chain of `id` is `id → … → root`. Any `d` on `id`'s chain is by definition on `b`'s chain — the assertion is a structural identity on any rooted acyclic tree. `dom_refl` (line 118): `dominates(b, b)` returns true on the first loop iteration (`b == d`). `idom_dominates_node` (line 122): `dominates(idom(b), b)` finds `idom(b)` after exactly one `dom.idom` hop. `check_antisym` (line 106–112): in an acyclic tree a node cannot be both ancestor and descendant of another; can only fail if the idom map has a cycle. Crucially, the test accesses `ssa.dom_tree` but never accesses `ssa.cfg` (which is a public field on `SsaFunction`), so the CFG structure is entirely ignored during verification. Only `entry_dominates` (line 119) — asserting the root is an ancestor of every reachable block — constitutes a real constraint that a wrong idom mapping could violate.

summary: Table row for DominatorTree poset/idom overclaims conformance depth: the test is circular (uses idom chain to verify idom chain), never checks against CFG edges, and omits an idom_unique check.
evidence: Two independently confirmed defects: (1) The local `dominates()` helper (dominator_conformance.rs:68–87) walks `dom.idom()` links to determine dominance — the same idom data structure being validated. Every subsequent assertion (`check_antisym`, `check_transitivity`, `dom_refl`, `entry_dominates`, `idom dominates node`) feeds through this helper, so all checks verify internal tree consistency, not correctness against CFG path semantics. No code in the test file ever re-reads `bb.successors` or reconstructs CFG-path reachability after `build_ssa`; the function's edge information is discarded. A `build_ssa` implementation that produces a self-consistent but semantically wrong tree (e.g., idoms pointing to wrong blocks) would pass all 4 000 random-CFG runs. The documentation at line 68 pairs the label "poset/idom" with the single conformance file, implying both aspects are machine-checked against the Rust implementation.

summary: Comment claims "possibly-overlapping fields" but the random_struct function never generates overlapping fields due to its sequential cursor-based construction. While overlapping fields are valid per the Coq TInfo.v spec and correctly handled by the Rust implementation, this edge case is never exercised in 200K test iterations.
evidence: Line 37-38: "Build a random flat struct: ascending, possibly-gapped, possibly-overlapping fields". However, in lines 44-55, cursor advances as: cursor = offset + width (end of field), then cursor += gap (gap ∈ [0,3]), so next offset = cursor + gap >= prior_end. Fields are strictly non-overlapping by construction. TInfo.v lines 45-46 state: "The selection proofs do NOT assume the field list is sorted", and theorem best_fit_tightest (lines 117-120) proves the highest-offset-wins property for overlapping containment. Rust tinfo.rs line 244 implements this: "Some(prev) if f.offset > prev.offset => best = Some(f)". The implementation correctly handles overlapping fields, but the test never generates them.

summary: Test header claims immediate-dominator uniqueness is verified, but test code does not exercise the idom_unique theorem
evidence: Lines 5–6 list "immediate-dominator uniqueness" as a tested property. The Coq theorem `idom_unique` (DominatorTree.v:164–165) proves that if two nodes d1 and d2 both satisfy the idom definition for a node n, they must mutually dominate each other (dominates d1 d2 ∧ dominates d2 d1). The test via `check_tree_laws` (lines 114–127) validates reflexivity, entry-dominance, transitivity along the idom chain, and antisymmetry of distinct blocks. However, it contains no code that (a) identifies alternative idom candidates by the definition (strictly dominates AND is the closest such dominator), (b) asserts multiple candidates exist, or (c) verifies they mutually dominate. The BTreeMap data structure structurally enforces one stored idom per node, but that is an implementation detail, not a test of the algorithm's correctness in selecting the unique idom. A bug in `build_ssa` that assigns an incorrect immediate dominator (wrong but dominating node) would not be caught by the existing test.

summary: Header falsely attributes 'struct natural align = max of field aligns' to DataLayout.v

This claim propagates into check_struct_align (line 141, "max-field-align rule" comment) and datalayout_struct_bounds_and_align (line 150, doc comment citing DataLayout.v for a property that does not exist there).

summary: datalayout_array_size_and_align is tautological: both assertions reduce to the implementation comparing itself to itself with no independent oracle
evidence: Lines 117–129 assert `dl.type_size(&arr) == es.checked_mul(len)` and `dl.type_align(&arr) == dl.type_align(&elem)` where `arr = Type::Array { element: Box::new(elem.clone()), size: Some(len) }`. Confirmed in data_layout.rs: `type_size` for `Type::Array { element, size: Some(count) }` is defined as `self.type_size(element)?.checked_mul(*count)` (line 62), and `type_align` for `Type::Array { element, .. }` is defined as `self.type_align(element)` (line 85). Both LHS calls dispatch into the same code path as the RHS expressions — the test is evaluating `f(wrap(elem, len)) == f_inline(elem, len)` where `f(wrap(...))` literally IS `f_inline` by definition. The assertions cannot fail unless a bug in one branch of the match arm affects only one side, which is structurally impossible here since there is only one call per function.

summary: Test doc comment attributes the max-field-align rule to DataLayout.v, which proves no such theorem.
evidence: layout_conformance.rs:150 reads: "/// Mirrors DataLayout.v `struct_size_bounds_member` + the max-field-align rule." struct_size_bounds_member is indeed a real theorem (DataLayout.v:121). However, the "max-field-align rule" (struct align >= every field align, enforced at runtime by check_struct_align at lines 141-148) has no corresponding theorem in DataLayout.v. LStruct is defined as `LStruct (members : list (Z * lty)) (alog : Z)` (line 22) with `alog_of (LStruct _ a) = a` (line 38) — struct alignment is an external parameter, not derived from member alignments, so no such property can be (or is) proven. The "Mirrors ... DataLayout.v" phrasing therefore falsely implies machine-checked backing for the struct-align check.

summary: Function-level `///` doc comment on `calibrate_dwarf_offsets` still describes the OLD acceptance condition (`d_matches > zero_matches`) after the implementation was changed to `zero_matches == 0 && d_matches >= 2`.

summary: Self-contradicting comment block: first paragraph describes a different condition than the second paragraph and neither fully matches the actual predicate
